 On 27 August Robespierre was elected as president of his section and explained in a letter to Le Moniteur Universel two motives: "I could not be the judge of those of which I was the adversary; but I had to remember that if they were the enemies of the fatherland, they had also declared themselves mine. This maxim, good in all circumstances, is especially applicable to this one: the justice of the people must bear a character worthy of it; it must be imposing as well as prompt and terrible.  
The exercise of these new functions was incompatible with that of representative of the Commune which had been entrusted to me; it was necessary to choose; I remained at the post where I was, convinced that it was there that I should currently serve the fatherland."[149]  
 The average age of the 24 deputies from Paris was 43. Robespierre was 34, Danton 33 and Marat 49.  
 On 5 February 1791 Robespierre declared: "True religion consists in punishing for the happiness of all those who disturb society."[179]  
 All children would be taken away from their parents and placed in a boarding school from the age of five, until the age of eleven for girls for girls, twelve for boys, and subjected to work. "The boys will be trained in addition to the handling of weapons."[233]  
 Four articles by Robespierre affirm the unity of the human race, universal male suffrage, the need for solidarity between the peoples, and the rejection of kings.[239]  
 On 16 March Robespierre was sharply critical of Amar's report, which presented the scandal around Fabre and Chabot as purely a matter of fraud. Robespierre insisted that it was a foreign plot, demanded that the report be re-written, and used the scandal as the basis for rhetorical attacks on William Pitt the Younger whom he believed was involved.[295]  
 On 27 March on the proposal of Barère the armée revolutionnaire, for seven months active in Paris and surroundings, was disbanded, except their artillery.[300][301][302][303] Their infantry and cavalry seem to be merged with other regiments.  

 On 9 Thermidor Vadier used a letter—supposedly found under the mattress of Théot—as an opportunity to attack Robespierre and his beliefs.[404] This letter announced to him that his mission had been prophesied in Ezekiel, that the re-establishment of religion, freed of priests, was owing to him.[405] Vadier becoming increasingly trivial was stopped by Tallien.[406]

 He signed 542 arrests, especially in 1794. Most of the arrests came from Bertrand Barère, Lazare Carnot and Pierre Louis Prieur.[454]

On 27 August Robespierre was elected as president of his section and explained in a letter to Le Moniteur Universel two motives: "I could not be the judge of those of which I was the adversary; but I had to remember that if they were the enemies of the fatherland, they had also declared themselves mine. This maxim, good in all circumstances, is especially applicable to this one: the justice of the people must bear a character worthy of it; it must be imposing as well as prompt and terrible.  
The exercise of these new functions was incompatible with that of representative of the Commune which had been entrusted to me; it was necessary to choose; I remained at the post where I was, convinced that it was there that I should currently serve the fatherland."[149]

opened.information:
Source: https://www.cathstan.org/culture/new-comic-book-novel-tells-story-of-father-emil-kapaun-army-chaplain-and-korean-war-pow
Title: New comic book novel tells story of Father Emil Kapaun, Army chaplain and Korean War POW - Catholic Standard
Chunks: 0,1
A nonprofit dedicated to supporting the U.S. Army has released a graphic novel highlighting the story and service of Father Emil Kapaun, the Catholic military chaplain who gave his life in a prisoner-of-war camp during the Korean War and has an active cause for canonization.
Since 2018, the Association of the United States Army, a nonprofit dedicated to supporting the U.S. Army through education and professional development initiatives, has released four graphic novels every year. The comic books seek to highlight the heroic lives and stories of Army Medal of Honor recipients.
This fall, the organization chose to feature the story of Father Kapaun, who received the Medal of Honor posthumously in 2013. Father Kapaun is the first military chaplain to be featured in the comic book series, which was released Sept. 23.
“I was doing research for a different graphic novel and came across the story of Father Kapaun, and his life really piqued my interest,” Joseph Craig, director of AUSA Book Program, told OSV News. “The more I learned about him, the more fascinating the story became. Based on the reception we are receiving about this particular issue, we are finding other people agree with that.”
Drawn and written by comic book professionals who have previously worked on Marvel and DC Comics projects, the new, eight-page comic presents Father Kapaun’s story in an engaging, accurate manner.
“These people really know how to make a story come to life and they really do Father Kapaun’s story justice,” Craig said. “We also work with a lot of military historians who volunteer their time to review the materials, to make sure we are getting the details all right. These are remarkable nonfiction stories that don’t need any embellishment.”
“As long as we present these stories in a straightforward way, people are going to love them,” he said.
Ordained in 1940 as a priest of the Diocese of Wichita, Kansas, Father Kapaun served as a military chaplain during World War II and the Korean War. While deployed in Korea, he was forced to surrender with his unit to Chinese forces. He was sent to a prisoner-of-war camp in North Korea where he continued to minister and serve his fellow POWs until he fell ill and died in May 1951. He held the rank of captain.

The cause for his canonization was formally opened in 1993, and in February of this year, he was declared “Venerable.”
“When you read about his selflessness, that alone is so inspirational,” Craig said. “His bravery on the battlefield as well as his spiritual compassion to his troops and in the prison camp was incredible. It’s a story that really reaches across generations and across all different peoples as Army fans are finding his story inspirational while Catholics and other believers are drawing spiritual nourishment from this story.”
Despite its short length, Craig hopes that readers will be inspired by Father Kapaun’s story and will be encouraged to do additional research about this priest’s inspirational life.
“These books center on the Medal of Honor citation and they are only eight pages long so we can only give a brief glimpse into these remarkable stories,” Craig said. “We hope that we present it in such an interesting way that it makes the reader want to learn more about Father Kapaun.”

TO SECURE PROMPT ATTENTION, ALL CORRESPONDENCE SHOULD BE ADDRESSED TO THE COMPANY American Book Company New York Cincinnati Chicago Publishers of School and College Text-books 521-531 Wabash Ave., Chicago, Oct. 24, 1896. 189 Pres. B. Cluff, Jr., Brigham Young College, Provo City, Utah. Dear Sir:- Your esteemed favor of the 21st inst. has been received, and in response to your request we take pleasure in mailing to you, for examination with a view to introduction, a copy of Roark*s Psychology in Education, and ask the acceptance of the same with our c cmpliments • The list price is $1, less 10X on introductory orders for class supplies, express charges paid. Commending the book to your favor, and inviting your further correspondence, we remain Very truly yours, AMERICAN BOOK COMPANY

TO SECURE PROMPT ATTENTION, ALL CORRESPONDENCE SHOULD BE ADDRESSED TO THE COMPANY American Book Company New York Cincinnati Chicago Publishers of School and College Text-books 521-531 Wabash Ave., Chicago, Oct. 24, 1896. 189 Pres. B. Cluff, Jr., Brigham Young College, Provo City, Utah. Dear Sir:- Your esteemed favor of the 21st inst. has been received, and in response to your request we take pleasure in mailing to you, for examination with a view to introduction, a copy of Roark*s Psychology in Education, and ask the acceptance of the same with our c cmpliments • The list price is $1, less 10X on introductory orders for class supplies, express charges paid. Commending the book to your favor, and inviting your further correspondence, we remain Very truly yours, AMERICAN BOOK COMPANY

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia
_London Review of Books_[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/4/41/Lrb17aug2006vol28no16.jpg/250px-Lrb17aug2006vol28no16.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Lrb17aug2006vol28no16.jpg)  
Editor Jean McNicol, Alice Spawls  
Categories[Literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literature "Literature"), [history](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History "History"), [ideas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idea "Idea")[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-1)

Language English  
Website[www.lrb.co.uk](https://www.lrb.co.uk/)  
[ISSN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ISSN_(identifier) "ISSN (identifier)")[0260-9592](https://www.worldcat.org/search?fq=x0:jrnl&q=n2:0260-9592)

The _**London Review of Books**_ (_**LRB**_) is a British [literary magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_magazine "Literary magazine") published semimonthly that features articles and essays on [fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiction "Fiction") and [non-fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction "Non-fiction") subjects, which are usually structured as [book reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_review "Book review").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-eday-2)

The _London Review of Books_ (_LRB_) was founded in 1979,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-eday-2) when publication of _[The Times Literary Supplement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times\_Literary\_Supplement "The Times Literary Supplement")_ was suspended during the year-long [lock-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockout_(industry) "Lockout (industry)") at _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-lrb_about-3) The _LRB_'s founding editors were [Karl Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Miller "Karl Miller"), then professor of English at [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London"); [Mary-Kay Wilmers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary-Kay_Wilmers "Mary-Kay Wilmers"), formerly an editor at _The Times Literary Supplement_; and [Susannah Clapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susannah_Clapp "Susannah Clapp"), a former editor at [Jonathan Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Cape "Jonathan Cape"). For its first six months, the _LRB_ appeared as an insert in _[The New York Review of Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Review\_of\_Books "The New York Review of Books")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-4) It became an independent publication in May 1980. Its political stance has been described by [Alan Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Bennett "Alan Bennett"), a prominent contributor, as "consistently radical".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-5)

Unlike _The Times Literary Supplement_ (TLS), the majority of the articles the _LRB_ publishes (usually fifteen per issue) are long essays. Some articles in each issue are not based on books, while several short articles discuss film or exhibitions. Political and social essays are frequent. The magazine is headquartered in [Bloomsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury "Bloomsbury"), London.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-eday-2)
Wilmers took over as editor in 1992 and remained as editor for almost 30 years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-FloodJan21-6) She was succeeded by Jean McNicol and Alice Spawls in 2021.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-FloodJan21-6) Average circulation per issue for January to December 2023 was 74,743.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-7)
In January 2010, _The Times_ wrote that the _London Review_ was £27M in debt to the Wilmers' family trust, although the trust had "no intention of the lender seeking repayment of the loan in the near future".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-8)
The **London Review Bookshop** opened in Bloomsbury in May 2003, and the Cake Shop next door in November 2007 (closed September 2024). The bookshop is used as a venue for author presentations and discussions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-lrb_about-3)

In 2011, when [Pankaj Mishra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pankaj_Mishra "Pankaj Mishra") criticised [Niall Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niall_Ferguson "Niall Ferguson")'s book _Civilisation: The West and the Rest_ in the _LRB_, Ferguson threatened to sue for libel.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-10)
In 2023, the [Hebrew Writers Association in Israel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hebrew_Writers_Association_in_Israel "Hebrew Writers Association in Israel") openly published a protest response to the letter of support for Gaza that was published in the journal, and called writers and artists around the world to support the freeing of the kidnapped.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-11)
In January 2024, _A Hitch in Time: Reflections Ready for Reconsideration_, an anthology of [Christopher Hitchens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christopher_Hitchens "Christopher Hitchens")'s writings between 1983 and 2002 for _The London Review of Books_, was published.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-NYT-20240101-12)

_**The Spectator**_ is a weekly British political and cultural [news magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_magazine "News magazine").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-:1-1) It was first published in July 1828,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-FirstNumber-2) making it the oldest surviving magazine in the world.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-3)_The Spectator_ is politically [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_Kingdom "Conservatism in the United Kingdom"), and its principal subject areas are politics and culture. Alongside columns and features on current affairs, the magazine also contains arts pages on books, music, opera, film, and TV reviews. It had an average circulation of 107,812 as of December 2023, excluding [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-4)

Editorship of the magazine has often been a platform to high office in the [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") in the United Kingdom; its past editors include [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") (1999–2005) and other former cabinet members [Ian Gilmour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Gilmour "Ian Gilmour") (1954–1959), [Iain Macleod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Macleod "Iain Macleod") (1963–1965), and [Nigel Lawson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Lawson "Nigel Lawson") (1966–1970). The former Conservative [MP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)")[Michael Gove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Gove "Michael Gove") took over from [Fraser Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraser_Nelson "Fraser Nelson") as editor on 4 October 2024.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-:0-7)

Today, the magazine is a print-digital hybrid. In 2020, _The Spectator_ became the longest-lived current affairs magazine in history (overtaking _[The Gentleman's Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gentleman's\_Magazine "The Gentleman's Magazine")_, which published from 1731 to 1922), and was also the first magazine ever to publish 10,000 issues.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-9) In September 2024, _The Spectator_ was acquired by British hedge fund manager [Paul Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Marshall_(investor) "Paul Marshall (investor)"), owner of [UnHerd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UnHerd "UnHerd") and co-owner of [GB News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GB_News "GB News").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-10)

### Robert Stephen Rintoul
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Spectator&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Robert Stephen Rintoul")]
_The Spectator_'s founder, Scottish reformer [Robert Stephen Rintoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stephen_Rintoul "Robert Stephen Rintoul"), former editor of the _[Dundee Advertiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee\_Courier\_&\_Argus "Dundee Courier & Argus")_ and the London-based _[Atlas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlas\_(newspaper) "The Atlas (newspaper)")_, launched the paper on 6 July 1828.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-FirstNumber-2)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-11) Rintoul consciously revived the title from the celebrated, if short-lived, daily publication by [Joseph Addison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Addison "Joseph Addison") and [Richard Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Steele "Richard Steele").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-13) As he had long been determined "to edit a perfect newspaper",[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Beach_Thomas_1928-14) Rintoul initially insisted on "absolute power"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Beach_Thomas_1928-14) over content, commencing a long-lasting tradition of the paper's editor and proprietor being one and the same person. Although he wrote little himself, "every line and word passed through the [alembic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alembic "Alembic") of his brain."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-15)

### Robert Stephen Rintoul
_The Spectator_'s political outlook in its first thirty years reflected Rintoul's [liberal-radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_radicalism "Classical radicalism") agenda.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Blake-16) Despite its political stance, it was widely regarded and respected for its non-partisanship, in both its political and cultural criticism. Rintoul initially advertised his new title as a "family paper", the euphemistic term for a journal free from strong political rhetoric, but events soon compelled him to confess that it was no longer possible to be "a mere Spectator". Two years into its existence, _The Spectator_ came out strongly for wide-reaching parliamentary reform: it produced supplements detailing vested interests in the Commons and Lords, coined the well-known phrase "The Bill, the whole Bill and nothing but the Bill", and helped drive through the [Great Reform Act of 1832](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832"). Virulently anti-[Tory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tory "Tory") in its politics, _The Spectator_ strongly objected to the appointment of the [Duke of Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Wellesley,_1st_Duke_of_Wellington "Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington") as prime minister, condemning him as "a Field Marshal whose political career proves him to be utterly destitute of political principle– whose military career affords ample evidence of his stern and remorseless temperament."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-17)

### Robert Stephen Rintoul
The paper spent its first century at premises on Wellington Street (now [Lancaster Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_Place "Lancaster Place")). Despite its robust criticism of the Conservative Party leader [Robert Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Peel "Robert Peel") for several years, _The Spectator_ rallied behind him when he split the Tory party by successfully repealing the [Corn Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corn_Laws "Corn Laws"). Rintoul's fundamental principles were freedom of the individual, freedom of the press and freedom of trade, of religious tolerance and freedom from blind political adherence. The magazine was vocal in its opposition to the [First Opium War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Opium_War "First Opium War") (1839–1842), commenting that "all the alleged aims of the expedition against China are vague, illimitable, and incapable of explanation, save only that of making the Chinese pay the opium-smugglers."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-18) The magazine further wrote: "There does not appear to be much glory gained in a contest so unequal that hundreds are killed on one side and none on the other. What honour is there in going to shoot men, certain that they cannot hurt you? The cause of the war, be it remembered, is as disreputable as the strength of the parties is unequal. The war is undertaken in support of a co-partnery of opium-smugglers, in which the [Anglo-Indian Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") may be considered as the principal partner."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-19)

### Robert Stephen Rintoul
In 1853, _The Spectator_'s lead book reviewer [George Brimley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Brimley "George Brimley") published an anonymous and unfavourable notice of [Charles Dickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens "Charles Dickens")'s _[Bleak House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleak\_House "Bleak House")_, typical of the paper's enduring contempt for him as a "popular" writer "amusing the idle hours of the greatest number of readers; not, we may hope, without improvement to their hearts, but certainly without profoundly affecting their intellects or deeply stirring their emotions."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-20) Rintoul died in April 1858, having sold the magazine two months earlier. The circulation had already been falling, under particular pressure from its new rival, _The Saturday Review_. Its new owner, the 27-year-old John Addyes Scott, kept the purchase quiet, but Rintoul's death made explicit the change of guard. His tenure was unremarkable, and subscribers continued to fall.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-21) By the end of the year, Scott sought his escape, selling the title for £4,200 in December 1858 (equivalent to £451,238 in 2025) to two British-based Americans, James McHenry and [Benjamin Moran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Moran "Benjamin Moran"). While McHenry was a businessman, Moran was an assistant secretary to the American ambassador, [George M. Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_M._Dallas "George M. Dallas"); they saw their purchase as a means to influence British opinion on American affairs.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-22)

### Robert Stephen Rintoul
The editor was [Thornton Leigh Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thornton_Leigh_Hunt "Thornton Leigh Hunt"), a friend of Moran who had also worked for Rintoul. Hunt was also nominally the purchaser, having been given the necessary monies in an attempt by McHenry and Moran to disguise the American ownership. Circulation declined with this loss of independence and inspirational leadership, as the views of [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"), then President of the United States, came to the fore. Within weeks, as the last pre-American ownership issue appears to have been that of 25 December 1858. the editorial line followed Buchanan's pronouncements in being "neither pro-[slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States") nor pro-[abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist"). To unsympathetic observers Buchanan's policy seemed to apportion blame for the impasse on the slavery question equally on pro-slavery and abolitionist factions – and rather than work out a solution, simply to argue that a solution would take time. _The Spectator_ now would publicly support that 'policy'".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Fulton-23) This set it at odds with most of the British press, but gained it the sympathy of expatriate Americans in the country. Richard Fulton notes that from then until 1861, "the _Spectator_'s commentary on American affairs read like a Buchanan administration propaganda sheet." and that this represented a _volte-face_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Fulton-23) Under Hunt's tenure, _The Spectator_ may even have been steered by financial support from the court of [Napoleon III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III "Napoleon III").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-24)

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
For his first year as proprietor, [John Evelyn Wrench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Wrench "Evelyn Wrench") appointed John (Jack) Atkins his editor, who had worked on the paper for the last two decades, acting as editor during Strachey's recurrent bouts of illness. But the relationship did not work: as Atkins lamented to his long-standing friend, [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"), Wrench "continually wants to interfere and he is very ignorant".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-33) Wrench duly took over the editorship in 1926, successfully channeling the enthusiasm of Strachey. His global connections helped secure interviews with [Henry Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford "Henry Ford"), [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi") and [Benito Mussolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini "Benito Mussolini"). Perhaps his most remembered achievement as editor of _The Spectator_ was the campaign to ease [unemployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployment_in_the_United_Kingdom "Unemployment in the United Kingdom") in the mining town of [Aberdare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdare "Aberdare"), one of the worst hit by the crisis of 1928, when joblessness reached 40% in [South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales "South Wales"). Within three months, the paper's appeal for the town's relief raised over £12,000 (equivalent to £651,789 in 2025).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31) A statuette of an Aberdare miner, presented in gratitude to _The Spectator_, still sits in the editor's office, bearing the inscription: "From the Townsfolk of Aberdare in Grateful Recognition: 'The Greatest of These is Love'".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-34)

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
Wrench retired as editor in 1932 (he remained the magazine's proprietor), appointing the political editor [Wilson Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Harris_(journalist) "Wilson Harris (journalist)") his successor. Under Harris _The Spectator_ became increasingly outspoken on [developing international politics in the 1930s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_relations_(1919%E2%80%931939) "International relations (1919–1939)"), in particular on the rise of [fascism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism"). Beneath a reader's letter referring to the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party") as "peaceful, orderly and kindly", Harris printed the following reply:
> No facts in recent history are established more incontestably... than the numerous cases of murder, assault, and various forms of intimidation for which the National Socialist Party in Germany has been responsible... The [organized economic boycott of the Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_boycott_of_Jewish_businesses "Nazi boycott of Jewish businesses") is the climax. _The Spectator_ has consistently shown itself a friend of Germany, but it is a friend of freedom first. Resort to violence is not condoned by styling it revolution.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-35)

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
Harris broadly supported the [European foreign policy of the Chamberlain ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_foreign_policy_of_the_Chamberlain_ministry "European foreign policy of the Chamberlain ministry") and [Neville Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Chamberlain "Neville Chamberlain")'s [appeasement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeasement "Appeasement"). He praised the [Munich Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement "Munich Agreement"), explaining later that he believed "even the most desperate attempt to save the peace was worthwhile".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31) Harris abandoned the newspaper's support for appeasement after the [Kristallnacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristallnacht "Kristallnacht") pogrom, which Harris wrote "obliterated the word appeasement."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-36) When the conflict broke, the team abandoned their Gower Street office for [Harmondsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmondsworth "Harmondsworth"), but within a few days decided to return to London: the basement caught fire from shrapnel, and the printers were [bombed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz"), but the paper continued to appear each week. Although the Second World War required _The Spectator_ to downgrade its size and paper quality, its readership doubled during the conflict, exceeding 50,000. From 1945 to 1950, Harris served as MP for [Cambridge University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Cambridge University (UK Parliament constituency)"); although he stood as an independent, this was the first formal overlap between _The Spectator_ and the House of Commons.

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
In February 1947, when a fuel shortage suspended the publication of weekly magazines, _The Spectator_ appeared in an abridged form over two successive Thursdays on page 2 of the _[Daily Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mail "Daily Mail")_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-38)

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
In 1954, Wrench and his co-owner [Angus Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_Watson_(entrepreneur) "Angus Watson (entrepreneur)") sold _The Spectator_ to the barrister [Ian Gilmour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Gilmour "Ian Gilmour"), who restored the _Spectator_ tradition of simultaneously acting as editor. Having a libertarian and pro-European outlook, he "enlivened the paper and injected a new element of irreverence, fun and controversy".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Blake-16) He was critical of both [Anthony Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Eden "Anthony Eden")'s and [Harold Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Macmillan "Harold Macmillan")'s governments, and while supporting the Conservatives was also friendly to [Hugh Gaitskell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Gaitskell "Hugh Gaitskell") and [Gaitskellism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaitskellism "Gaitskellism").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-royjenkins-auto-39) Gilmour lent _The Spectator_'s voice to the campaign to end [capital punishment in Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_Britain "Capital punishment in Britain"), writing an incensed leader attacking the hanging of [Ruth Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ellis "Ruth Ellis") in 1955, in which he claimed "Hanging has become the national sport", and that the home secretary [Gwilym Lloyd George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwilym_Lloyd_George "Gwilym Lloyd George"), for not reprieving the sentence, "has now been responsible for the hanging of two women over the past eight months".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31)

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
_The Spectator_ opposed Britain's involvement in the [Suez Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Crisis "Suez Crisis") in 1956, strongly criticising the government's handling of the debacle. The paper went on to oppose Macmillan's government's re-election in the [1959 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_United_Kingdom_general_election "1959 United Kingdom general election"), complaining: "The continued Conservative pretence that Suez was a good, a noble, a wise venture has been too much to stomach... the Government is taking its stand on a solid principle: 'Never admit a mistake.'"[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31) The paper also says that it was influential in campaigning for the [decriminalisation of homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decriminalisation_of_homosexuality "Decriminalisation of homosexuality").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-40) It gave vocal support to the proposals of the [Wolfenden Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfenden_Committee "Wolfenden Committee") in 1957, condemning the "utterly irrational and illogical" old laws on homosexuality: "Not only is the law unjust in conception, it is almost inevitably unjust in practice."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31)

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
In March 1957, Jenny Nicholson, a frequent contributor, wrote a piece on the [Italian Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Socialist_Party "Italian Socialist Party") congress in [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice"), which mentioned three [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") politicians ([Aneurin Bevan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aneurin_Bevan "Aneurin Bevan"), [Richard Crossman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Crossman "Richard Crossman"), and [Morgan Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Phillips "Morgan Phillips")) "who puzzled the Italians by filling themselves like tanks with whisky and coffee".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-41) All three sued for libel, the case went to trial, and _The Spectator_ was forced to make a large payment in damages and costs, a sum well over the equivalent of £150,000 today.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld-42) It has since emerged that "all three plaintiffs, to a greater or lesser degree, perjured themselves in court".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld-42)

### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
Gilmour gave up the editorship in 1959, in part to abet his chance of selection as a Conservative MP. He appointed his deputy [Brian Inglis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Inglis "Brian Inglis"), who introduced to the magazine a fresh spirit of political satire. In 1959—much to the embarrassment of Gilmour (who remained the owner)—_The Spectator_ advised either voting for the Liberal Party or tactically abstaining. Despite a marked increase in sales, Gilmour felt that _The Spectator_ was losing its political edge, so replaced him in 1962 with [Iain Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Hamilton_(journalist) "Iain Hamilton (journalist)"). Hamilton successfully balanced a keener focus on current affairs with some more raucous contributions as the young team behind _[Private Eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private\_Eye "Private Eye")_ were commissioned to write a mock eight-page _Child's Guide to Modern Culture_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-43) Much to the shock of Hamilton and the _Spectator_ staff, Gilmour replaced Hamilton in 1963 with [Iain Macleod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Macleod "Iain Macleod"), the Conservative MP who had resigned from the cabinet on the controversial appointment of Sir [Alec Douglas-Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Douglas-Home "Alec Douglas-Home") to succeed [Harold Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Macmillan "Harold Macmillan") as prime minister. A widely circulated letter, signed by _Spectator_ journalists and board members, berated Gilmour for mistreating an admired editor and appointing an active politician who could jeopardise the independence of the magazine: "We believe strongly that _The Spectator_, with its long and honourable history of independent opinion, should not be tossed about at the whim of the proprietor or lose its independence by identification with a narrow political faction."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-44)

### "The Tory Leadership" article
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Spectator&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: \"The Tory Leadership\" article")]
Two months into his post, in January 1964, Macleod intensified the shock by revealing the behind-the-scenes machinations of the Conservative party. In a long article entitled "The Tory Leadership", ostensibly a review of a new book (_The Fight for the Tory Leadership_) by [Randolph Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Churchill "Randolph Churchill"), Macleod laid out his version of events in great detail. In disclosing, from the horse's mouth, the mysterious circumstances of Douglas-Home's appointment, the article caused an immediate sensation. Churchill's book was all but obliterated by the review, which said that "four fifths" of it "could have been compiled by anyone with a pair of scissors, a pot of paste and a built-in prejudice against Mr [Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rab_Butler "Rab Butler") and Sir [William Haley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Haley "William Haley")".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-46) That week's edition, bearing the headline "Iain Macleod, What Happened", sold a record number of copies.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-48)

### Nigel Lawson, George Gale, and Harry Creighton
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Spectator&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Nigel Lawson, George Gale, and Harry Creighton")]
The "Tory Leadership" article prompted a furious response from many _Spectator_ readers and caused Macleod, for a time, to be shunned by political colleagues. He eventually regained his party's favour, however, and rejoined the shadow cabinet in the same year. On his appointment as Shadow Chancellor in 1965, he stepped down as editor on the last day of the year, to be replaced by [Nigel Lawson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Lawson "Nigel Lawson"). Sometimes called "The Great Procrastinator" because of his tendency to leave writing leaders until the last minute,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Blake-16) Lawson had been City editor for _[The Sunday Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sunday\_Telegraph "The Sunday Telegraph")_ and Alec Douglas-Home's personal assistant during the [1964 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_United_Kingdom_general_election "1964 United Kingdom general election"). In 1966, largely due to Lawson, _The Spectator_ opposed America's increasing military commitment in [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). In a signed article he estimated "the risks involved in an American withdrawal from Vietnam are less than the risks in escalating a bloody and brutal war".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld-42)

_**The Spectator**_ is a weekly British political and cultural [news magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/News_magazine "News magazine").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-:1-1) It was first published in July 1828,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-FirstNumber-2) making it the oldest surviving magazine in the world.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-3)_The Spectator_ is politically [conservative](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservatism_in_the_United_Kingdom "Conservatism in the United Kingdom"), and its principal subject areas are politics and culture. Alongside columns and features on current affairs, the magazine also contains arts pages on books, music, opera, film, and TV reviews. It had an average circulation of 107,812 as of December 2023, excluding [Australia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australia "Australia").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-4)
texts.2: Editorship of the magazine has often been a platform to high office in the [Conservative Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conservative_Party_(UK) "Conservative Party (UK)") in the United Kingdom; its past editors include [Boris Johnson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Johnson "Boris Johnson") (1999–2005) and other former cabinet members [Ian Gilmour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Gilmour "Ian Gilmour") (1954–1959), [Iain Macleod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Macleod "Iain Macleod") (1963–1965), and [Nigel Lawson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Lawson "Nigel Lawson") (1966–1970). The former Conservative [MP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_Parliament_(United_Kingdom) "Member of Parliament (United Kingdom)")[Michael Gove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Gove "Michael Gove") took over from [Fraser Nelson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fraser_Nelson "Fraser Nelson") as editor on 4 October 2024.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-:0-7)
texts.3: Today, the magazine is a print-digital hybrid. In 2020, _The Spectator_ became the longest-lived current affairs magazine in history (overtaking _[The Gentleman's Magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Gentleman's\_Magazine "The Gentleman's Magazine")_, which published from 1731 to 1922), and was also the first magazine ever to publish 10,000 issues.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-9) In September 2024, _The Spectator_ was acquired by British hedge fund manager [Paul Marshall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Marshall_(investor) "Paul Marshall (investor)"), owner of [UnHerd](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UnHerd "UnHerd") and co-owner of [GB News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GB_News "GB News").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-10)

### Robert Stephen Rintoul
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Spectator&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Robert Stephen Rintoul")]
_The Spectator_'s founder, Scottish reformer [Robert Stephen Rintoul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Stephen_Rintoul "Robert Stephen Rintoul"), former editor of the _[Dundee Advertiser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dundee\_Courier\_&\_Argus "Dundee Courier & Argus")_ and the London-based _[Atlas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Atlas\_(newspaper) "The Atlas (newspaper)")_, launched the paper on 6 July 1828.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-FirstNumber-2)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-11) Rintoul consciously revived the title from the celebrated, if short-lived, daily publication by [Joseph Addison](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Addison "Joseph Addison") and [Richard Steele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Steele "Richard Steele").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-13) As he had long been determined "to edit a perfect newspaper",[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Beach_Thomas_1928-14) Rintoul initially insisted on "absolute power"[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Beach_Thomas_1928-14) over content, commencing a long-lasting tradition of the paper's editor and proprietor being one and the same person. Although he wrote little himself, "every line and word passed through the [alembic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alembic "Alembic") of his brain."[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-15)
texts.5:
### Robert Stephen Rintoul
_The Spectator_'s political outlook in its first thirty years reflected Rintoul's [liberal-radical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classical_radicalism "Classical radicalism") agenda.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Blake-16) Despite its political stance, it was widely regarded and respected for its non-partisanship, in both its political and cultural criticism. Rintoul initially advertised his new title as a "family paper", the euphemistic term for a journal free from strong political rhetoric, but events soon compelled him to confess that it was no longer possible to be "a mere Spectator". Two years into its existence, _The Spectator_ came out strongly for wide-reaching parliamentary reform: it produced supplements detailing vested interests in the Commons and Lords, coined the well-known phrase "The Bill, the whole Bill and nothing but the Bill", and helped drive through the [Great Reform Act of 1832](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_Act_1832 "Reform Act 1832"). Virulently anti-[Tory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tory "Tory") in its politics, _The Spectator_ strongly objected to the appointment of the [Duke of Wellington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthur_Wellesley,_1st_Duke_of_Wellington "Arthur Wellesley, 1st Duke of Wellington") as prime minister, condemning him as "a Field Marshal whose political career proves him to be utterly destitute of political principle– whose military career affords ample evidence of his stern and remorseless temperament."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-17)
texts.6:
### Robert Stephen Rintoul
The paper spent its first century at premises on Wellington Street (now [Lancaster Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lancaster_Place "Lancaster Place")). Despite its robust criticism of the Conservative Party leader [Robert Peel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Peel "Robert Peel") for several years, _The Spectator_ rallied behind him when he split the Tory party by successfully repealing the [Corn Laws](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corn_Laws "Corn Laws"). Rintoul's fundamental principles were freedom of the individual, freedom of the press and freedom of trade, of religious tolerance and freedom from blind political adherence. The magazine was vocal in its opposition to the [First Opium War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Opium_War "First Opium War") (1839–1842), commenting that "all the alleged aims of the expedition against China are vague, illimitable, and incapable of explanation, save only that of making the Chinese pay the opium-smugglers."[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-18) The magazine further wrote: "There does not appear to be much glory gained in a contest so unequal that hundreds are killed on one side and none on the other. What honour is there in going to shoot men, certain that they cannot hurt you? The cause of the war, be it remembered, is as disreputable as the strength of the parties is unequal. The war is undertaken in support of a co-partnery of opium-smugglers, in which the [Anglo-Indian Government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") may be considered as the principal partner."[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-19)
texts.7:
### Robert Stephen Rintoul
In 1853, _The Spectator_'s lead book reviewer [George Brimley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Brimley "George Brimley") published an anonymous and unfavourable notice of [Charles Dickens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_Dickens "Charles Dickens")'s _[Bleak House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bleak\_House "Bleak House")_, typical of the paper's enduring contempt for him as a "popular" writer "amusing the idle hours of the greatest number of readers; not, we may hope, without improvement to their hearts, but certainly without profoundly affecting their intellects or deeply stirring their emotions."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-20) Rintoul died in April 1858, having sold the magazine two months earlier. The circulation had already been falling, under particular pressure from its new rival, _The Saturday Review_. Its new owner, the 27-year-old John Addyes Scott, kept the purchase quiet, but Rintoul's death made explicit the change of guard. His tenure was unremarkable, and subscribers continued to fall.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-21) By the end of the year, Scott sought his escape, selling the title for £4,200 in December 1858 (equivalent to £451,238 in 2025) to two British-based Americans, James McHenry and [Benjamin Moran](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Moran "Benjamin Moran"). While McHenry was a businessman, Moran was an assistant secretary to the American ambassador, [George M. Dallas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_M._Dallas "George M. Dallas"); they saw their purchase as a means to influence British opinion on American affairs.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-22)
texts.8:
### Robert Stephen Rintoul
The editor was [Thornton Leigh Hunt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thornton_Leigh_Hunt "Thornton Leigh Hunt"), a friend of Moran who had also worked for Rintoul. Hunt was also nominally the purchaser, having been given the necessary monies in an attempt by McHenry and Moran to disguise the American ownership. Circulation declined with this loss of independence and inspirational leadership, as the views of [James Buchanan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Buchanan "James Buchanan"), then President of the United States, came to the fore. Within weeks, as the last pre-American ownership issue appears to have been that of 25 December 1858. the editorial line followed Buchanan's pronouncements in being "neither pro-[slavery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_the_United_States "Slavery in the United States") nor pro-[abolitionist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abolitionist "Abolitionist"). To unsympathetic observers Buchanan's policy seemed to apportion blame for the impasse on the slavery question equally on pro-slavery and abolitionist factions – and rather than work out a solution, simply to argue that a solution would take time. _The Spectator_ now would publicly support that 'policy'".[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Fulton-23) This set it at odds with most of the British press, but gained it the sympathy of expatriate Americans in the country. Richard Fulton notes that from then until 1861, "the _Spectator_'s commentary on American affairs read like a Buchanan administration propaganda sheet." and that this represented a _volte-face_.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Fulton-23) Under Hunt's tenure, _The Spectator_ may even have been steered by financial support from the court of [Napoleon III](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Napoleon_III "Napoleon III").[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-24)
texts.15:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
For his first year as proprietor, [John Evelyn Wrench](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evelyn_Wrench "Evelyn Wrench") appointed John (Jack) Atkins his editor, who had worked on the paper for the last two decades, acting as editor during Strachey's recurrent bouts of illness. But the relationship did not work: as Atkins lamented to his long-standing friend, [Winston Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Winston_Churchill "Winston Churchill"), Wrench "continually wants to interfere and he is very ignorant".[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-33) Wrench duly took over the editorship in 1926, successfully channeling the enthusiasm of Strachey. His global connections helped secure interviews with [Henry Ford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Ford "Henry Ford"), [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi") and [Benito Mussolini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benito_Mussolini "Benito Mussolini"). Perhaps his most remembered achievement as editor of _The Spectator_ was the campaign to ease [unemployment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unemployment_in_the_United_Kingdom "Unemployment in the United Kingdom") in the mining town of [Aberdare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aberdare "Aberdare"), one of the worst hit by the crisis of 1928, when joblessness reached 40% in [South Wales](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Wales "South Wales"). Within three months, the paper's appeal for the town's relief raised over £12,000 (equivalent to £651,789 in 2025).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31) A statuette of an Aberdare miner, presented in gratitude to _The Spectator_, still sits in the editor's office, bearing the inscription: "From the Townsfolk of Aberdare in Grateful Recognition: 'The Greatest of These is Love'".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-34)
texts.16:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
Wrench retired as editor in 1932 (he remained the magazine's proprietor), appointing the political editor [Wilson Harris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Harris_(journalist) "Wilson Harris (journalist)") his successor. Under Harris _The Spectator_ became increasingly outspoken on [developing international politics in the 1930s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_relations_(1919%E2%80%931939) "International relations (1919–1939)"), in particular on the rise of [fascism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fascism "Fascism"). Beneath a reader's letter referring to the [Nazi Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Party "Nazi Party") as "peaceful, orderly and kindly", Harris printed the following reply:
> No facts in recent history are established more incontestably... than the numerous cases of murder, assault, and various forms of intimidation for which the National Socialist Party in Germany has been responsible... The [organized economic boycott of the Jews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_boycott_of_Jewish_businesses "Nazi boycott of Jewish businesses") is the climax. _The Spectator_ has consistently shown itself a friend of Germany, but it is a friend of freedom first. Resort to violence is not condoned by styling it revolution.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-35)
texts.17:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
Harris broadly supported the [European foreign policy of the Chamberlain ministry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_foreign_policy_of_the_Chamberlain_ministry "European foreign policy of the Chamberlain ministry") and [Neville Chamberlain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neville_Chamberlain "Neville Chamberlain")'s [appeasement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Appeasement "Appeasement"). He praised the [Munich Agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich_Agreement "Munich Agreement"), explaining later that he believed "even the most desperate attempt to save the peace was worthwhile".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31) Harris abandoned the newspaper's support for appeasement after the [Kristallnacht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kristallnacht "Kristallnacht") pogrom, which Harris wrote "obliterated the word appeasement."[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-36) When the conflict broke, the team abandoned their Gower Street office for [Harmondsworth](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmondsworth "Harmondsworth"), but within a few days decided to return to London: the basement caught fire from shrapnel, and the printers were [bombed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Blitz "The Blitz"), but the paper continued to appear each week. Although the Second World War required _The Spectator_ to downgrade its size and paper quality, its readership doubled during the conflict, exceeding 50,000. From 1945 to 1950, Harris served as MP for [Cambridge University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambridge_University_(UK_Parliament_constituency) "Cambridge University (UK Parliament constituency)"); although he stood as an independent, this was the first formal overlap between _The Spectator_ and the House of Commons.
texts.18:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
In February 1947, when a fuel shortage suspended the publication of weekly magazines, _The Spectator_ appeared in an abridged form over two successive Thursdays on page 2 of the _[Daily Mail](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daily\_Mail "Daily Mail")_.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-37)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-38)
texts.19:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
In 1954, Wrench and his co-owner [Angus Watson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angus_Watson_(entrepreneur) "Angus Watson (entrepreneur)") sold _The Spectator_ to the barrister [Ian Gilmour](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ian_Gilmour "Ian Gilmour"), who restored the _Spectator_ tradition of simultaneously acting as editor. Having a libertarian and pro-European outlook, he "enlivened the paper and injected a new element of irreverence, fun and controversy".[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Blake-16) He was critical of both [Anthony Eden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Eden "Anthony Eden")'s and [Harold Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Macmillan "Harold Macmillan")'s governments, and while supporting the Conservatives was also friendly to [Hugh Gaitskell](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hugh_Gaitskell "Hugh Gaitskell") and [Gaitskellism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaitskellism "Gaitskellism").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-royjenkins-auto-39) Gilmour lent _The Spectator_'s voice to the campaign to end [capital punishment in Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_punishment_in_Britain "Capital punishment in Britain"), writing an incensed leader attacking the hanging of [Ruth Ellis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ruth_Ellis "Ruth Ellis") in 1955, in which he claimed "Hanging has become the national sport", and that the home secretary [Gwilym Lloyd George](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwilym_Lloyd_George "Gwilym Lloyd George"), for not reprieving the sentence, "has now been responsible for the hanging of two women over the past eight months".[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31)
texts.20:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
_The Spectator_ opposed Britain's involvement in the [Suez Crisis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suez_Crisis "Suez Crisis") in 1956, strongly criticising the government's handling of the debacle. The paper went on to oppose Macmillan's government's re-election in the [1959 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1959_United_Kingdom_general_election "1959 United Kingdom general election"), complaining: "The continued Conservative pretence that Suez was a good, a noble, a wise venture has been too much to stomach... the Government is taking its stand on a solid principle: 'Never admit a mistake.'"[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31) The paper also says that it was influential in campaigning for the [decriminalisation of homosexuality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Decriminalisation_of_homosexuality "Decriminalisation of homosexuality").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-40) It gave vocal support to the proposals of the [Wolfenden Committee](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolfenden_Committee "Wolfenden Committee") in 1957, condemning the "utterly irrational and illogical" old laws on homosexuality: "Not only is the law unjust in conception, it is almost inevitably unjust in practice."[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld_1999-31)
texts.21:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
In March 1957, Jenny Nicholson, a frequent contributor, wrote a piece on the [Italian Socialist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Italian_Socialist_Party "Italian Socialist Party") congress in [Venice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice "Venice"), which mentioned three [Labour Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Labour_Party_(UK) "Labour Party (UK)") politicians ([Aneurin Bevan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aneurin_Bevan "Aneurin Bevan"), [Richard Crossman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Crossman "Richard Crossman"), and [Morgan Phillips](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morgan_Phillips "Morgan Phillips")) "who puzzled the Italians by filling themselves like tanks with whisky and coffee".[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-41) All three sued for libel, the case went to trial, and _The Spectator_ was forced to make a large payment in damages and costs, a sum well over the equivalent of £150,000 today.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld-42) It has since emerged that "all three plaintiffs, to a greater or lesser degree, perjured themselves in court".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld-42)
texts.22:
### Evelyn Wrench and Wilson Harris
Gilmour gave up the editorship in 1959, in part to abet his chance of selection as a Conservative MP. He appointed his deputy [Brian Inglis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Inglis "Brian Inglis"), who introduced to the magazine a fresh spirit of political satire. In 1959—much to the embarrassment of Gilmour (who remained the owner)—_The Spectator_ advised either voting for the Liberal Party or tactically abstaining. Despite a marked increase in sales, Gilmour felt that _The Spectator_ was losing its political edge, so replaced him in 1962 with [Iain Hamilton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Hamilton_(journalist) "Iain Hamilton (journalist)"). Hamilton successfully balanced a keener focus on current affairs with some more raucous contributions as the young team behind _[Private Eye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Private\_Eye "Private Eye")_ were commissioned to write a mock eight-page _Child's Guide to Modern Culture_.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-43) Much to the shock of Hamilton and the _Spectator_ staff, Gilmour replaced Hamilton in 1963 with [Iain Macleod](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iain_Macleod "Iain Macleod"), the Conservative MP who had resigned from the cabinet on the controversial appointment of Sir [Alec Douglas-Home](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alec_Douglas-Home "Alec Douglas-Home") to succeed [Harold Macmillan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harold_Macmillan "Harold Macmillan") as prime minister. A widely circulated letter, signed by _Spectator_ journalists and board members, berated Gilmour for mistreating an admired editor and appointing an active politician who could jeopardise the independence of the magazine: "We believe strongly that _The Spectator_, with its long and honourable history of independent opinion, should not be tossed about at the whim of the proprietor or lose its independence by identification with a narrow political faction."[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-44)
texts.23:
### "The Tory Leadership" article
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Spectator&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: \"The Tory Leadership\" article")]
Two months into his post, in January 1964, Macleod intensified the shock by revealing the behind-the-scenes machinations of the Conservative party. In a long article entitled "The Tory Leadership", ostensibly a review of a new book (_The Fight for the Tory Leadership_) by [Randolph Churchill](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Randolph_Churchill "Randolph Churchill"), Macleod laid out his version of events in great detail. In disclosing, from the horse's mouth, the mysterious circumstances of Douglas-Home's appointment, the article caused an immediate sensation. Churchill's book was all but obliterated by the review, which said that "four fifths" of it "could have been compiled by anyone with a pair of scissors, a pot of paste and a built-in prejudice against Mr [Butler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rab_Butler "Rab Butler") and Sir [William Haley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Haley "William Haley")".[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-45)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-46) That week's edition, bearing the headline "Iain Macleod, What Happened", sold a record number of copies.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-47)[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-48)
texts.24:
### Nigel Lawson, George Gale, and Harry Creighton
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=The_Spectator&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Nigel Lawson, George Gale, and Harry Creighton")]
The "Tory Leadership" article prompted a furious response from many _Spectator_ readers and caused Macleod, for a time, to be shunned by political colleagues. He eventually regained his party's favour, however, and rejoined the shadow cabinet in the same year. On his appointment as Shadow Chancellor in 1965, he stepped down as editor on the last day of the year, to be replaced by [Nigel Lawson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nigel_Lawson "Nigel Lawson"). Sometimes called "The Great Procrastinator" because of his tendency to leave writing leaders until the last minute,[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Blake-16) Lawson had been City editor for _[The Sunday Telegraph](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Sunday\_Telegraph "The Sunday Telegraph")_ and Alec Douglas-Home's personal assistant during the [1964 United Kingdom general election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1964_United_Kingdom_general_election "1964 United Kingdom general election"). In 1966, largely due to Lawson, _The Spectator_ opposed America's increasing military commitment in [Vietnam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"). In a signed article he estimated "the risks involved in an American withdrawal from Vietnam are less than the risks in escalating a bloody and brutal war".[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Spectator#cite_note-Courtauld-42)

texts.1: The _**London Review of Books**_ (_**LRB**_) is a British [literary magazine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literary_magazine "Literary magazine") published semimonthly that features articles and essays on [fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fiction "Fiction") and [non-fiction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non-fiction "Non-fiction") subjects, which are usually structured as [book reviews](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Book_review "Book review").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-eday-2)
texts.2: The _London Review of Books_ (_LRB_) was founded in 1979,[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-eday-2) when publication of _[The Times Literary Supplement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times\_Literary\_Supplement "The Times Literary Supplement")_ was suspended during the year-long [lock-out](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lockout_(industry) "Lockout (industry)") at _[The Times](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Times "The Times")_.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-lrb_about-3) The _LRB_'s founding editors were [Karl Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karl_Miller "Karl Miller"), then professor of English at [University College London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_College_London "University College London"); [Mary-Kay Wilmers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary-Kay_Wilmers "Mary-Kay Wilmers"), formerly an editor at _The Times Literary Supplement_; and [Susannah Clapp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susannah_Clapp "Susannah Clapp"), a former editor at [Jonathan Cape](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Cape "Jonathan Cape"). For its first six months, the _LRB_ appeared as an insert in _[The New York Review of Books](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_New\_York\_Review\_of\_Books "The New York Review of Books")_.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-4) It became an independent publication in May 1980. Its political stance has been described by [Alan Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alan_Bennett "Alan Bennett"), a prominent contributor, as "consistently radical".[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-5)
texts.3:
Unlike _The Times Literary Supplement_ (TLS), the majority of the articles the _LRB_ publishes (usually fifteen per issue) are long essays. Some articles in each issue are not based on books, while several short articles discuss film or exhibitions. Political and social essays are frequent. The magazine is headquartered in [Bloomsbury](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bloomsbury "Bloomsbury"), London.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-eday-2)
Wilmers took over as editor in 1992 and remained as editor for almost 30 years.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-FloodJan21-6) She was succeeded by Jean McNicol and Alice Spawls in 2021.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-FloodJan21-6) Average circulation per issue for January to December 2023 was 74,743.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-7)
In January 2010, _The Times_ wrote that the _London Review_ was £27M in debt to the Wilmers' family trust, although the trust had "no intention of the lender seeking repayment of the loan in the near future".[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-8)
The **London Review Bookshop** opened in Bloomsbury in May 2003, and the Cake Shop next door in November 2007 (closed September 2024). The bookshop is used as a venue for author presentations and discussions.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Review_of_Books#cite_note-lrb_about-3)

# John Lee, Night Editor of the Mail, dies suddenly at 58
*   **With paper for 28 years under editors Paul Dacre, Geordie Greig and Ted Verity**  
*   **Worked his way up starting as news sub-editor and rising to Night Editor in 2015**
By DAILY MAIL REPORTER
Published: 00:39 BST, 1 February 2023  | Updated: 11:20 BST, 1 February 2023
Share[Add us as a preferred source](https://google.com/preferences/source?q=dailymail.com)[15 comments](https://www.dailymail.com/news/article-11699075/John-Lee-Night-Editor-Mail-dies-suddenly-58.html#comments)
It is with great sadness that the Daily Mail announces the sudden death of Night Editor John Lee at the age of 58.
John, a brilliant and inspirational journalist, came from a newspaper-owning family in Huddersfield, West Yorkshire.
He worked on provincial titles including the Huddersfield Daily Examiner, the Bradford Telegraph and Argus, the [Brighton](https://www.dailymail.com/news/brighton/index.html) Argus and the Manchester Evening News before joining the Mail in [London](https://www.dailymail.com/news/london/index.html).

Ted Verity, Editor, Mail Newspapers, said: 'John was an exceptionally talented journalist who brought huge flair and his own inimitable personality to everything he did. He will be greatly missed.'
A close colleague said last night: 'John became a trusted and loyal friend over the 26 years we knew each other and was simply a joy to work with.
'Clever, funny and utterly unflappable, he had the perfect personality for a night editor – fascinated by the news agenda but with just enough cynicism not to be seduced by its tricks. We will all miss him hugely.'

# Daily Mail night editor John Lee dies suddenly at 58
Lee leaves a wife, Louise, and a daughter Georgina, herself a journalist with Channel 4 News.
By [Bron Maher](https://pressgazette.co.uk/author/bron-maher/)
![Image 7: John Lee, Daily Mail night editor from 2015.](https://pressgazette.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/sites/7/2023/02/John-Lee-e1675253763109-1038x778.jpg)

The [Daily Mail](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/daily-mail/) has announced “with great sadness” the sudden death of night editor John Lee aged 58.
Lee, described by the paper as “a brilliant and inspirational journalist”, came from a newspaper-owning family in Huddersfield.

# Daily Mail night editor John Lee dies suddenly at 58
Before making his way to the Mail, Lee worked at titles including the [Huddersfield Daily Examiner](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/huddersfield-examiner/), the Bradford Telegraph and Argus, the [Brighton Argus](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/the-argus/) and the [Manchester Evening News](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/manchester-evening-news/).
He worked at the Mail for 28 years under editors [Paul Dacre](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/paul-dacre/), [Geordie Greig](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/geordie-greig/) and Ted Verity, beginning as a news sub-editor. He was appointed night editor in 2015, a job the Mail said he “loved”.
Daily Mail editor [Ted Verity](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/daily-mail-editor-geordie-greig-steps-down-as-ted-verity-takes-charge-of-seven-day-operation/) said: “John was an exceptionally talented journalist who brought huge flair and his own inimitable personality to everything he did. He will be greatly missed.”
A close colleague said on Tuesday night: “John became a trusted and loyal friend over the 26 years we knew each other and was simply a joy to work with.
“Clever, funny and utterly unflappable, he had the perfect personality for a night editor – fascinated by the news agenda but with just enough cynicism not to be seduced by its tricks. We will all miss him hugely.”
Lee leaves a wife, Louise, an academic, and [a daughter Georgina](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/vicarious-trauma-journalists-ukraine/), herself a journalist with [Channel 4 News](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/channel-4-news/).

# Daily Mail night editor John Lee dies suddenly at 58
Before making his way to the Mail, Lee worked at titles including the [Huddersfield Daily Examiner](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/huddersfield-examiner/), the Bradford Telegraph and Argus, the [Brighton Argus](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/the-argus/) and the [Manchester Evening News](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/manchester-evening-news/).
He worked at the Mail for 28 years under editors [Paul Dacre](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/paul-dacre/), [Geordie Greig](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/geordie-greig/) and Ted Verity, beginning as a news sub-editor. He was appointed night editor in 2015, a job the Mail said he “loved”.
Daily Mail editor [Ted Verity](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/daily-mail-editor-geordie-greig-steps-down-as-ted-verity-takes-charge-of-seven-day-operation/) said: “John was an exceptionally talented journalist who brought huge flair and his own inimitable personality to everything he did. He will be greatly missed.”
A close colleague said on Tuesday night: “John became a trusted and loyal friend over the 26 years we knew each other and was simply a joy to work with.
“Clever, funny and utterly unflappable, he had the perfect personality for a night editor – fascinated by the news agenda but with just enough cynicism not to be seduced by its tricks. We will all miss him hugely.”
Lee leaves a wife, Louise, an academic, and [a daughter Georgina](https://pressgazette.co.uk/news/vicarious-trauma-journalists-ukraine/), herself a journalist with [Channel 4 News](https://pressgazette.co.uk/subject/channel-4-news/).

would be well within the contemplation of the [Foreign and Domestic Emoluments]

foreign governments absent congressional consent.  However, despite numerous indications that

In the modern age, the treatment of  honors received by Presidents John F. Kennedy and  
Barack Obama from foreign nations once again confirmed the broad scope of the Foreign  
Emoluments Clause.  In 1963, the Irish Government awarded President Kennedy honorary Irish  
citizenship.  Reiterating the conclusion that the Foreign Emoluments Clause was “directed  
against every kind of influence by foreign governments upon officers of the United States, based  
on our historic policies as a nation,” the DOJ determined that acceptance “would fall within the  
spirit, if not the letter” of the Clause’s prohibition.  48  President Kennedy declined the honor.  49  In  
2009, President Obama accepted the Nobel Peace Prize only after the DOJ determined that the  
selection process was independent from the influence of the Norwegian government.  In reaching  
this conclusion, however, the DOJ Office of Legal Counsel (OLC) once again affirmed that the  
Clause applies to the President because the “President surely ‘holds an Office of Profit or  
Trust.’”  50  President Obama promptly donated the $1.4 million Nobel Prize money to charity.  51
In advisory opinions issued during the modern era, the DOJ has broadly defined  
“emolument” as reaching the benefits, gains, or advantages that flow from transactional business  
relationships with foreign governments or entities, including private transactions.  52  Moreover,  
federal district courts that addressed this issue in cases brought against then  -President Trump  
have likewise concluded that the Clause reaches profits arising from private or “market”

## [PDF page 22]
transactions.  53  The opinions are consistent with the expansive language of the Clause, which  
refers to “any present, Emolument, Office, or Title, of any kind whatever  ,” and also the Framers’  
intent to protect against the possibility that foreign nations would propose personal business  
transactions with American federal officials to obtain preferential policy treatment from them.  54
FormerPresident Trump’s shocking departure from these deeply established and long-  
observed principles caused significant public controversy during his Administration.  Although  
he never sought c  ongressional permission to keep any of the millions of dollars he collected from  
foreign governments and foreign government-owned companies, the American public took  
notice of the rampant flow of funds to his businesses from these sources.  The attorneys general  
of the District of Columbia and Maryland, Members of Congress, several public interest groups,  
and others brought or supported legal actions to try to  stop these violations of the Foreign  
Emoluments Clause.  Ultimately, the lawsuits were never decided on the merits because the  
courts dismissed them on threshold  procedural grounds, including that the parties lacked legal  
standing to sue or that the litigation became moot after Donald Trump left office.  55
As one of those courts concluded with respect to former President Trump:
[S]ole or substantial ownership of a business that receives hundreds of thousands or  
millions of dollars a year in revenue from one of its hotel properties where foreign and  
domestic governments are known to stay (often with the express purpose of cultivating  
the President’s good graces) most definitely raises the potential for undue influence, and

the Committee, nor did he provide the basis for his statement  that private citizens were  
responsible for these stays.  He also did not explain whether these individuals were members of

Regardless of whether the stay labeled as the Sheikh Al Thani Family Extended Stay  
involved only private citizens, it would be reasonable to infer that the booking of a prolonged  
hotel stay—which ultimately yielded hundreds of thousands of dollars in payments to a Trump-  
owned business—using the name of the Qatari royal family was  intended to signal to The Trump  
Organization and to then-President Trump the country’s financial support of the President’s  
business at a time when Qatar was seeking then-President Trump’s support in a conflict that  
constituted a crisis to Qatar.  This is one more expenditure highlighting how  then-President  
Trump’s continued ownership of private businesses created  a magnet for foreign countries  
seeking to influence the foreign policy of the United States through payments to the President  
and his businesses.  This is precisely the kind of self-dealing that the U.S. Constitution seeks to  
prevent by prohibiting a President from receiving emoluments  “of any kind whatever” from  
foreign governments absent congressional consent.  However, despite numerous indications that  
this expensive stay involved members of Qatar  ’s royal family, given  the Ambassador  ’s  
representations to the Committee, this report does not include the expenditures at the Trump  
International Hotel by the Sheikh Al Thani Family among the total emoluments  paid  by Qatar to  
Trump-owned businesses.

According to the records provided to the Committee by Mazars, on four occasions  
between October 2017 and May 2018, the government of the United Arab Emirates (  U.A.E.)
